member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.ContentAddons
member.summary:
The content addons connecting clients are told to download.
The active list is the server config's serverbrowser.content_addons merged with whatever every loaded plugin declares through , de-duplicated and kept in that order. Declaring an addon from a plugin means it no longer has to be listed in the server config ahead of time - loading the plugin is enough.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.CBaseEntity.ApplyDamage(DeadworksManaged.Api.CTakeDamageInfo)
member.summary: Deals damage to this entity the way the game does, so the target's resistances and other damage modifiers apply. is called for it.

remarks.para: Set to the kind of damage you are dealing (for example or ), since it decides which modifiers apply. It starts out as .
The final amount is written back into , so use a new for each call. Reusing one, for example for every target of an area attack, applies the modifiers again each time.
Calling this from inside an handler triggers that handler again, so guard against loops (for example when reflecting damage back at the attacker).

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.CBaseEntity.TakeDamage(DeadworksManaged.Api.CTakeDamageInfo)

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.CBeam
member.summary: A glowing line between two points in the world that every player can see. Create one with , or a whole box or path at once with and .

remarks.para: Beams glow like a laser: they brighten whatever is behind them, so they always look a little see-through, and the world's lighting shades them. They can't be made solid or fullbright. Black beams are invisible, and lowering the alpha makes a beam fainter. Change the color at any time with .
A beam stays until you remove it (, or for a list) or the map changes.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.CCitadelPlayerController.RemoveWithPawns
member.summary:
Removes this player from the game completely: their hero, any other pawn they control (such as a spectator's observer pawn), and this controller, together in the same tick.
By default a player who leaves keeps their controller and hero, so they can reconnect to them, and their portrait stays in the top bar. Call this from to drop them instead. Don't remove the hero or the controller on its own: either one left behind crashes clients or the server. To remove a player who is still connected, them.

member.summary:
Gives an imbuable item to this pawn and imbues it into the ability in - the managed equivalent of giveitem <item> <slot>.
Nothing is granted unless the whole operation can succeed, so a rejected pairing never leaves the pawn holding an unattached item. Use when you need to know why it failed.
Internal item name, e.g. "upgrade_echo_shard".
Ability to imbue into. The four imbuable slots are through (indices 0-3).
Should the enhanced version of the item be given Returns the new item entity, or null on failure.

member.summary: Gives every map the match start dl_midtown has: a countdown in base, then everyone launched down their lane's zipline (choose lanes with ). Off by default, when only dl_midtown starts that way and any other map goes straight into the match with everyone in base.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.GameRules.SetWaitingForPlayersRoster(System.UInt32,System.UInt32)
member.summary: Overrides the roster used by the engine's internal WaitingForPlayersToJoin readiness check. The engine's own roster is populated by matchmaking/party data, which is always empty on a direct-connect dedicated server, so the check (and the counts it caches into the client-networked HUD fields) reflects a real target instead of always reading empty/zero. The state advances once >= . Pass a of 0 to disable the override and restore the engine's native behavior. This is native global state, not a field on the game rules entity; it is persists across map changes and is cleared on plugin unload.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.GameRules.SetGameStartTime(System.Single)
member.summary: Sets m_flGameStartTime, which the match clock ( and the client's HUD timer) is computed relative to. On a server without real matchmaking, this field is never reset once the pregame flow actually reaches GameInProgress, so the clock counts from map load instead of from when the match really starts.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.GameRules.SetGameStateEndTime(System.Single)
member.summary: Sets m_flGameStateEndTime, which drives the client's countdown display for states that show one (e.g. PreGameWait's "Game starting..."). The engine's own ChangeGameState only writes a real value here when an internal eligibility check passes; on servers where that check never passes, the field is left at a sentinel and the client shows no countdown number.

member.typeparam: The protobuf message type. Must be registered in .
member.param: The message to send.
Which players should receive this message.
member.exception: Thrown if has no registered message ID.
member.param: Which net-channel buffer to use. Reliable guarantees ordered delivery but disconnects the client if the server outruns its acks (NETWORK_DISCONNECT_RELIABLEOVERFLOW) — it degrades off a cliff, not gracefully. Unreliable simply drops the packet under pressure, which is the right trade for latest-wins traffic such as telemetry or HUD state. Anything that must not be lost — layout, ordering, handshakes, or one fragment of a multi-part message — has to stay reliable.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.PlayerCamera
member.summary: Moves a player's camera without moving their hero: pull it back, zoom, point it somewhere else and hold it there. Get one from .

remarks.para: Every call is a timed change to one : a lerp moves it from one value to another, and holds it where it is. When a change ends, the setting snaps back to what the game wants, so follow a lerp with to keep its end value. Pass a delay to line up several changes back to back in one go, like the legs of a fly-through.

Your changes go in a group, unless you pass your own id, and removes one group without touching the game's own camera effects. When two changes to the same setting overlap, the higher priority wins, and beats the game's.

The camera still bumps into walls, so pointing it at something behind geometry pulls it in close. And the world is still loaded around the hero, not the camera, so a camera sent far away can show missing scenery. Move the hero along with it if that matters.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.PlayerCamera.DefaultPriority
member.summary: The priority your changes get when you don't pass one. It's above the game's own, so yours win.

member.summary: Moves the camera's look-at point from to over seconds, with full control over the motion, then snaps it back. Use to keep the end value. is the short form.

Where the move starts. Pass where the camera looks now for a smooth move.

From 0 to 1. Below 0.5 starts slow and speeds up, above 0.5 starts fast and slows down.
From 0 to 1. Above 0.5 eases in and out, below 0.5 does the opposite. 0.5 for both keeps a steady speed.
Seconds to wait before starting.
The group this change goes in, for .

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI
member.summary:
Entry point for the UI message manager. Use to obtain a handle for a logical UI panel; the panel id binds to the panorama-side panel script registered with the same id via DW.registerPanel({ id: "..." }).
A panel stays up until you destroy it, the player leaves, or the map changes. Every panel is gone on a new map, so treat any you were tracking as closed in and show them again as players arrive.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.RatePerSecond
member.summary: Per-recipient subtitle send rate, in frames/s. Defaults to 24.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.BurstSize
member.summary: Per-recipient burst capacity (token-bucket size). Defaults to 24.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.BytesPerSecond
member.summary:
Per-recipient wire budget in bytes/s. Defaults to 16 KB/s.
This is the budget that matters: frames go out on the reliable net channel, which disconnects the client on overflow rather than throttling. Raise it only with real players on a real server, watching for choke and drops.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.MaxFramesPerSecond
member.summary:
Frames per second this channel can actually deliver, derived from and the client's six-caption display pool. Read-only.
Pace recurring updates against this. Offering frames faster than the channel drains does not increase throughput — it just grows the queue and adds latency, because a frame is only as useful as the moment it arrives. Your achievable byte rate is roughly MaxFramesPerSecond × bytes-per-update; to go faster, send more per frame rather than more frames.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.CaptionLengthSeconds
member.summary:
How long each caption frame lives on the client, in seconds. Defaults to 0.2.
This governs throughput, not bandwidth. The client renders at most six captions at a time and silently discards any beyond that, so the channel tops out at 6 / CaptionLengthSeconds frames per second — about 5/s at the game's default linger, which is why the transport felt slow regardless of rate or frame size. The send rate is clamped to stay inside this automatically.
Lower means more throughput but less time for the client to build its panel and for the mod to read it. Do not go near a frame time.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.CaptionLingerSeconds
member.summary:
The client's cc_linger_time, which is added to every caption's own length to get its expiry. Defaults to 0.3, matching what the addon asserts on the client.
This is not a knob you set to change client behaviour — the addon owns that. It exists so tells the truth. If you ship an addon with a different CC_LINGER, set the same value here or the channel will pace itself against a pool that recycles slower than it thinks.

member.name: P:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.MaxFrameLength
member.summary:
Bytes of wire payload per caption frame. Defaults to 3800.
Hard-capped just under 4000: the client copies caption text into a fixed char[4096] stack buffer with no bounds check, so larger frames corrupt its stack. Larger frames are otherwise strictly better — each frame costs one usermessage, so fewer/fatter frames means less reliable-channel pressure for the same payload.

member.name: E:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UI.ClientResync
member.summary:
A client discarded its UI and needs its layouts re-sent. The argument is the player slot.
The client tears everything down if server frames stop arriving for a few seconds — a hitch is enough — and it cannot rebuild on its own, because layouts live on the server. Any plugin that ships a panel should re-send it here, otherwise that player's UI stays blank until they reconnect. Re-sending is idempotent: precache/show simply replaces whatever the client had.

It reports in once their game has loaded the map, usually within a few seconds of , so false straight after joining doesn't mean they lack it. It also reads false for a moment while their UI rebuilds after a hitch.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIPanel.SetStyle(DeadworksManaged.Api.RecipientFilter,System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
Change one style property on a node already in the panel's tree, without rebuilding it.
is the node's Id, resolved client-side. Patches coalesce latest-wins per (node, property), so calling this every frame is safe: offering updates faster than the channel drains costs nothing but intermediate values. has no such coalescing — driving it per-frame grows an unbounded backlog and the panel falls progressively further behind.
For anything whose path is known in advance, prefer one patch plus a CSS transition over a stream of them:
UI.Panel("hud").SetStyle(to, "bar", "transition-duration", "30s"); UI.Panel("hud").SetStyle(to, "bar", "width", "0%");
The client then interpolates at its own framerate, which is smoother than this channel could ever be and costs nothing after the first patch.

member.summary:
Change to over , letting the client interpolate.
This is the form to reach for whenever the destination is known in advance. A thirty-second bar is one call, not one call per frame: the client animates at its own rate, the result is smoother than this channel could deliver, and it keeps running through a server hitch because the server is no longer involved.
Equivalent to declaring on the node and then calling , and safe to call on a node that already declares one.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.PanelSnapshot
member.summary:
What it takes to rebuild one panel on one client from nothing.
The client discards its entire UI whenever server frames stop arriving for a few seconds, and it cannot rebuild alone — layouts only exist server-side. Rather than making every plugin remember to handle that (forget it once and that player's UI is dead until reconnect, silently), the channel keeps the last structural op per panel and replays it.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.Pending
member.summary:
A pending value plus the point in the ordered stream at which a plugin asked for it.
Values coalesce latest-wins, so a plugin's call order cannot be recovered from the dictionary itself. Without the stamp the drain has to guess, and it guessed wrong in both directions: flushing everything ahead of the next ordered op sent values at a tree that BuildLayout had not created yet, and flushing everything behind it let a value survive a Clear that was issued after it.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.Pending.#ctor(System.String,System.Int64)
member.summary:
A pending value plus the point in the ordered stream at which a plugin asked for it.
Values coalesce latest-wins, so a plugin's call order cannot be recovered from the dictionary itself. Without the stamp the drain has to guess, and it guessed wrong in both directions: flushing everything ahead of the next ordered op sent values at a tree that BuildLayout had not created yet, and flushing everything behind it let a value survive a Clear that was issued after it.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.CaptionSlots
member.summary: Captions the client will render at once. sub_181953220 stops collecting at 6, and only collected items get a Panorama panel — so a 7th concurrent caption is not delayed, it is lost.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.CaptionPoolUtilisation
member.summary: Fraction of the pool to actually use. At exactly 6 / lifetime the pool sits permanently full and any frame-time jitter drops a caption, so aim for roughly four of the six slots in steady state.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.CaptionLingerSeconds
member.summary:
How long a caption lingers on top of its own length. The client computes a caption's expiry as cc_linger_time + len, so our <len:N> frames occupy a slot for N + linger, not N — and the pool recycles that much slower.
This value is sent to the client on every heartbeat and the addon asserts it as cc_linger_time, so the two halves can't drift. Raising it costs throughput and buys margin against a slow Panorama frame dropping a caption unseen.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.SafeCaptionRate
member.summary:
Frames per second the client can actually absorb. Exceeding this loses data silently, which is worse than being slow, so Tick clamps to it.
Divides by lifetime, not length: a slot is held for the caption's length plus the linger. Ignoring the linger overstated this by several times at the stock value, which is why the channel felt slower than its numbers said.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.EnqueueChunks(DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.Slot,System.String,System.Boolean)
member.param: Requested channel. A multi-frame message is forced back to reliable regardless: the client reassembles chunks by wire-id and flag, so a dropped fragment does not degrade the message, it destroys it (and strands the reassembly buffer until the id is reused). Only a message that fits in a single frame can safely be unreliable.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.CaptionLengthSeconds
member.summary:
Per-caption lifetime, in seconds, injected as <len:N> markup.
This is the single most important throughput knob, and it is not about bandwidth. CCitadelHudSubtitles (client.dll sub_181953220) walks the caption item list and stops collecting at 6 items:
if (v7 >= 6) break;
Only those six ever get a Panorama panel, so items 7+ are invisible to the mod no matter how fast we send. Effective throughput is therefore 6 / lifetime. Left alone, lifetime is cc_linger_time (~1.2s), which caps the channel at ~5 captions/sec regardless of rate or frame size.
<len:N> is parsed out of the caption text by sub_1816C64E0, which sets the item's death time to cc_linger_time + N — linger is added, not replaced. Both halves are ours: this one rides in the caption text, and linger is sent on the heartbeat for the client to assert.
Lifetime is the whole story for throughput, and it also sets frame size: a plugin filling a byte budget puts budget / framerate in each frame, so a long lifetime means fewer, fatter captions. Those are more expensive for the client to lay out, since the subtitle Label is html="true". Do not drop this near a Panorama frame time — an item that expires before the UI next runs is never rendered, and what is never rendered can never be read.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.Acknowledge(System.Int32,System.String,System.String)

A runtime addon reported in (routed from dw_ui ~|addon|<panel>|<state>).
The bootstrap sends ok/fail for whether the layout resolved at all, and the addon's own script sends ready once it registers. Those are genuinely different: a mounted VPK with a broken script reports ok but never ready.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.RequestResync(System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary:
The client tore its UI down and has nothing left (routed via UIBootstrap from dw_ui ~|resync|<token>).
The client's heartbeat watchdog destroys every panel when frames stop arriving — a server hitch is enough. Without this the server still believed the client was acked, so it kept streaming Set ops at a client that had no panels to apply them to and never re-sent the layouts: the UI stayed dead until reconnect. Resetting to the pre-handshake state re-runs the hello, and lets plugins put their layouts back.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.ReplayInto(DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.Slot)
member.summary:
Re-queues the retained structure and field values for one client.
Faithful for the precache/show, build and load-xml panels that make up almost everything. It is NOT faithful for panels built up with Append/Erase: those are deltas against a tree, and we keep only the base, so the panel returns to its last full layout without the incremental children. Such a panel is flagged and its owner should rebuild it from — hence the event still exists.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIChannel.OnMapStart
member.summary: A new map is starting: forget every panel sent on the old one. Players stay connected through a map change, so otherwise their game would get the old panels back when it rebuilds its UI after the load, with no plugin tracking them any more to close them. The new token also clears any client whose UI survived the load.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UILz77
member.summary:
Tiny LZ77-style compressor used as a final pass over the encoded BuildLayout payload. After the field encoder + style tokenizer have done their thing, the wire stream still contains a lot of cross-field repetition (the same compressed button style fragment appears once per button, etc.). LZ77 catches those automatically without any per-tree analysis.
Wire format:
Literal byte: passes through unchanged.
Backref: \x1e <o1> <o2> <len> — four bytes total. o1 and o2 are base-94 digits in 33..126 encoding the offset minus one (so offsets 1..8836 fit). len is the same encoding, mapped to a match length of code + 4 (4..97).
Literal escape (rare — \x1e never appears in our encoded trees in practice): doubled to \x1e\x1e.
\x1e (Record Separator) is in the same ASCII control-char family as \x1f (Unit Separator), which the existing protocol already round-trips successfully through the closed-caption transport.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIStyleCompressor
member.summary:
Token-based compressor for the entire encoded BuildLayout payload (not just style fields). Replaces a fixed table of common substrings — CSS property names, common CSS values, and a handful of HUD-specific UI patterns — with two-byte codes of the form ^X, where X is one ASCII letter or digit.
The escape marker ^ is exceedingly rare in real style/text/id content, so the round-trip is lossless in practice. Authors who put ^X sequences (caret followed by alphanumeric) into label text or IDs may see them rewritten on the client.
Applied once to the whole field-separated payload after . The encoder builds style strings without whitespace from (name, value) pairs, so no minification is needed here.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UITreeEncoder
member.summary:
Encodes a tree as a flat sequence of fields separated by \x1f. JSON was tried first but the closed-caption transport mangles some of its structural characters; this format uses only \x1f as a separator (already proven to round-trip via the existing Set/Clear/Raw ops).
**Empty fields are encoded as the single character ~** so the wire payload never contains two consecutive \x1f bytes — there's evidence the caption layer collapses runs of separators, which would silently shift fields out of alignment downstream. The bootstrap interprets a lone ~ field as empty when reading back.
The payload begins with a deduplicated style table so a repeated style (e.g. the row style shared by every scoreboard row) is shipped once, not once per node. Only styles used by 2+ nodes go in the table — a one-off style stays inline because the table-plus-reference (~4 chars) would be pure overhead vs. just emitting the CSS directly. Each node's style field is one of: ~ (empty), @N (table reference), or an inline CSS string. Layout on the wire:
styleCount \x1f style0 \x1f style1 \x1f ... \x1f <node fields...>
Per node, eight fields in fixed order, then the node's children laid out recursively in the same shape:
type — single char: p plain, v vertical, h horizontal, L label, B button, I image.
id — element id (or ~).
style — ~ for empty or @N referencing the style table.
text — Label/Button text, or Image src path (or ~).
event — Button click spec, event[,arg1,arg2,...] (or ~).
hover — styles applied while the pointer is over the node, same encoding as style (or ~).
press — styles applied while the pointer is held down, same encoding again (or ~).
child_count — decimal integer.
The node arity is fixed, so the encoder and the client bootstrap have to ship together.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UITreeEncoder.BaseStyleCss(DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UINode)
member.summary: A node's own styles plus any transitions it declared, which Panorama expresses as three parallel comma-separated lists.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire
member.summary:
Wire-format encoders for the UI message protocol.
Two layers stack on top of each other: 1. Logical message: panel_id \x1f op \x1f arg0 \x1f arg1 ... 2. Subtitle frame: u~ <id> <flag> <payload> (≤ 50 chars total)
One logical message is chunked into 1+ subtitle frames sharing a wire-id character. Flags: '*' = single-chunk, '+' = first, '=' = continuation, '!' = last.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.CaptionHardLimit
member.summary: Hard ceiling imposed by the client, not by us. The caption processor (client.dll sub_1816C64E0) copies caption text into a fixed char[4096] stack buffer, and the copy loop advances its write pointer with no bounds compare — a segment at or above 4096 bytes overwrites the client's stack. Never raise this.

member.name: F:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.SubtitleMaxLength
member.summary:
Wire length of one caption frame. Nothing in the caption pipeline truncates: the item text reaches the panel as a whole CUtlString and is handed to SetDialogVariable("subtitle_text") intact. The old value of 50 matched the width: 400px visual line-wrap in citadel_hud_subtitles.css, which only affects rendering — the Label's .text still returns the full string.
Bigger frames are also *cheaper* on the wire: every frame costs a usermessage plus protobuf framing, and frames are sent BUF_RELIABLE (see NativeSendNetMessage), so fewer/fatter frames means strictly less reliable-channel pressure for the same payload.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EscapeWire(System.String)
member.summary: Rewrites a logical message so the wire form contains no character the caption transport mangles. Mirrored by unescapeWire in dw_bootstrap.js. Applied to the whole message before chunking, so the \x1f field separators and the LZ77 envelope both pass through unharmed (neither 0x1E nor 0x1F is in the escaped set).

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EncodeSet(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.Collections.Generic.KeyValuePair{System.String,System.String}})
member.summary: Encodes a Set op: panel \x1f s \x1f lz77(k \x1f v \x1f k \x1f v ...). The k/v payload is LZ77-compressed because the caption transport silently collapses runs of repeated characters (consecutive spaces, duplicate separators). LZ77 backref-encodes those runs so the values survive the wire intact — the same mechanism that keeps Build payloads lossless. Token compression is intentionally skipped: Set values are arbitrary user data and could legitimately contain strings that match CSS-property tokens.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EncodeStyle(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.ValueTuple{System.String,System.String,System.String}})
member.summary:
Encodes a Style op: panel \x1f y \x1f lz77(tokens(node \x1f prop \x1f value \x1f ...)).
Token-compressed, unlike . Set carries arbitrary user data that could legitimately contain a ^X sequence and be rewritten by the detokenizer; a style payload is CSS property names and CSS values, where a caret does not occur. The saving is large precisely because the table is CSS properties — background-color is one byte plus the escape.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EncodeAppend(System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Encodes an Append op: panel \x1f a \x1f parentId \x1f compressedSubtree. parentId is held outside the LZ77 envelope so the bootstrap can peel it off with a single indexOf(\x1f) before decompressing the rest. member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EncodeErase(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Encodes an Erase op: panel \x1f e \x1f targetId. Bootstrap removes the matching child via DeleteAsync and also clears any auto-bind state under that id.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.EncodeHeartbeat(System.String,System.Int64,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Encodes a Heartbeat op: ~ \x1f h \x1f token \x1f seq \x1f version [\x1f a]. The reserved panel id ~ never collides with a real id (it's the empty-field placeholder). is the stable per-session id the client watches for change (reconnect detection); increments every send so each heartbeat's caption text is unique and can't be swallowed by the client's burst-dedup / dwLastText layers. appends a trailing a field: the pre-handshake hello, asking the bootstrap to reply dw_ui ~|ack|token to prove its caption pipeline is live.

member.name: M:DeadworksManaged.Api.UI.UIWire.Chunk(System.String,System.Char)
member.summary:
Escapes a logical message into wire form, then splits it into 1+ subtitle frames using a single-char wire id. Single-chunk uses '*' flag; multi-chunk uses '+' / '=' / '!'.
Escaping happens before splitting so a frame boundary can never land inside an escape pair — and because ESC only ever appears as the first byte of a two-byte pair (a literal ESC is written as ESC 'D'), a chunk whose last character is ESC is unambiguously mid-pair and gives that byte back to the next frame.

member.name: T:DeadworksManaged.Api.Utils.Zone
member.summary: A box in the world that tells you when players walk into it and out of it, through and . Use it for checkpoints, start and finish lines, reset areas, safe areas, or anything else you'd otherwise check by hand every frame.

remarks.para: Zones check each player's position every game tick. The position is at the hero's feet, so to catch a player standing in an area, start the box a little below the floor and go up to about head height. Dead players, and players who haven't picked a hero yet, count as outside every zone.

Because positions are only checked once a tick, a fast player (dashing, on a zipline) can cross a thin zone between two checks without ever being inside. Make zones that catch moving players, like finish lines, at least 100 units deep in the direction they're crossed.
A zone keeps working until you call or your plugin unloads. To show it in the world, draw it with CBeam.CreateBox(zone.Mins, zone.Maxs).
